findings.title: Do not pipe an unpinned remote script into sh
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN fetches https://example.com/install.sh at build time and executes it as root via `sh` with no version pin, checksum, or signature. HTTPS only authenticates the hostname, not the script bytes; whatever that URL returns (today or on a later rebuild) becomes arbitrary root code in every image. example.com is not a software distribution channel, so this is unsigned third-party execution on the image supply chain.

findings.title: Fail the image build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL` omits `--fail`, so HTTP 4xx/5xx still exit 0 and the body is executed. Docker's default SHELL is `/bin/sh -c` (no `pipefail`); on a transport-level curl failure the pipeline's status is `sh`'s status. Empty stdin to `sh` exits 0, so the RUN layer succeeds and `CMD ["/app"]` ships an image as if the installer ran. `-s` also drops curl's error text from build logs.

findings.title: Stop unpinned curl|sh remote install in image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN downloads https://example.com/install.sh and pipes it straight into sh with no checksum, signature, or version pin. Whatever that URL (or an -L redirect) serves at build time runs as root in the build and is baked into the image — a classic supply-chain RCE. curl -sL also hides errors, and the pipeline is evaluated by Docker's default /bin/sh -c without pipefail, so only sh's status is checked: a failed download feeds empty stdin, sh exits 0, and Docker commits a successful layer as if the install ran.

findings.title: Stop executing unpinned remote install.sh during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN downloads https://example.com/install.sh and pipes it into sh as root, with no checksum, signature, version pin, or integrity check. curl -L follows redirects, so a compromised origin, MITM, or redirect can inject arbitrary code into every built image. This is a live supply-chain execution path, not a comment or unused helper.

findings.title: Fail the image build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: curl -sL has no --fail, -s hides curl errors, and Docker's default SHELL [/bin/sh, -c] does not set pipefail, so RUN takes the exit status of sh only. A network failure leaves sh with empty stdin (empty script exits 0); an HTTP error body is executed as a script. The build continues and tags an image as if the installer ran.

findings.title: Do not discard Load errors in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value. LoadOrDefault blank-assigns that error and returns v, so this exported API maps both cases (and any other Load failure) to "". Callers cannot tell failure from a legitimate empty string and will treat the fallback as real data.

findings.title: Wait for result goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Run used to send every j*2 on results before returning, so a caller could close(results) (or otherwise treat return as 'all produced') safely. The new per-job goroutines are not waited on, so Run returns while sends are still in flight. close(results) after Run is then a send-on-closed-channel panic, and any receive/len snapshot taken immediately after return can miss values. The signature is still a sync producer (exported, send-only channel, no WaitGroup/done), so callers have no other completion signal. Concurrent sends also make result order non-deterministic versus the previous in-order loop.

findings.title: Join worker goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous loop sent every `j*2` on `results` before `Run` returned, so return was a completion barrier (safe to close or drain a full batch). The new `go func` workers are never joined: `Run` returns as soon as the goroutines are started. A caller that closes `results` after `Run` (the normal producer-done pattern) races child sends against that close → `send on closed channel` in a child goroutine, which crashes the process and is not recoverable by the caller. A caller that inspects a buffered `results` immediately after return can also see a partial batch. Send order is no longer jobs-order, so positional pairing of jobs to results is wrong even when all values eventually arrive.

findings.title: Wait for spawned job goroutines before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run sent every doubled job on results before returning, so a caller could close(results) or read exactly len(jobs) values after Run returned. The new go func sends asynchronously and Run returns as soon as the goroutines are scheduled. A caller that close(results) after Run panics (send on closed channel). A caller that only receives after Run returns can observe fewer than len(jobs) values. There is no WaitGroup, channel close, or ctx cancel path, so those goroutines also outlive the call.

findings.title: Keep delete authorization as admin AND same tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported delete gate changed from conjunction to disjunction. Substituting the four truth-table cases: (isAdmin=false, tenantId match) previously denied and now allows any tenant member to delete any record in the tenant; (isAdmin=true, tenantId mismatch) previously denied and now allows an admin to delete another tenant's record. Both are unauthorized deletes relative to the previous contract. (isAdmin=true, match) and (isAdmin=false, mismatch) are unchanged.

findings.title: Require admin and matching tenant to delete records
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported gate changed from `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` to `||`. Substituting live inputs: (1) non-admin, same tenant `{isAdmin:false, tenantId:T}` vs `{tenantId:T}` was false and is now true, so any tenant member may delete any record in the tenant; (2) admin, other tenant `{isAdmin:true, tenantId:T1}` vs `{tenantId:T2}` was false and is now true, so an admin session may delete another tenant's records. Previously only same-tenant admins could delete. That is an authorization bypass on the public delete predicate (and a data-loss path for every caller).

findings.title: Restore admin∧tenant delete auth; OR is a privilege bypass
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous gate required both session.isAdmin and session.tenantId === record.tenantId, so only a tenant-scoped admin could delete. Replacing && with || makes the function true for every same-tenant session (isAdmin=false is enough) and for every admin regardless of tenant (tenant mismatch is enough). That removes the admin-only restriction and tenant isolation on an exported delete-authorization API. RecordRef.ownerId / Session.userId are never consulted, so this is not an owner check.

Substituting: parse_positive_int(-1) → -1 → charge(-1) → -100 → total_cents([-1]) → -100, which a caller of parse_positive_int must treat as a valid positive quantity.

findings.title: Do not mutate caller DataFrame after dropping defensive copy
findings.whyItBreaks: apply_values previously copied the input (`result = df.copy()`), assigned into the copy, and returned that independent frame, so the caller's DataFrame was left unchanged. The new body does `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` and `return df`. pandas `.loc` assignment mutates the receiver in place, so the argument and the return value are now the same object. Any caller that still holds the input (or later mutates the return value) sees aliased writes; passing a slice/view can also make the loc assignment fail to persist (SettingWithCopy), whereas the copy made the returned frame a real, updated object.

findings.title: Decrement stock before awaiting save to prevent oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads remaining, then awaits store.save before this.stock.set. In JavaScript that await yields, so overlapping reserve() calls for the same SKU all observe the same remaining, all persist remaining-1, all return true, and in-memory stock is left too high. Previously the check-and-decrement was synchronous and could not interleave. Example: load(sku, 1) then Promise.all([reserve(sku), reserve(sku)]) both resolve true and stock ends at 0 instead of one failure.

findings.title: Claim stock before awaiting store.save to prevent oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve reads remaining and gates on remaining <= 0, then awaits store.save before this.stock.set. await yields, so a second reserve(sku) reads the still-unupdated Map, passes the same guard, and also save(remaining - 1) + returns true. Base reserve was synchronous (no interleaving on the event loop); this PR introduces the yield. With load(sku, 1) then Promise.all([reserve(sku), reserve(sku)]), both resolve true and both persist 0, so two units are reserved from one.

findings.title: Decrement stock before await to prevent concurrent oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() is now async and awaits store.save() while this.stock still holds the pre-reserve count. On a single-threaded event loop that await is a yield: two overlapping reserve(sku) calls both read remaining=N (e.g. 1), both pass remaining<=0, both persist N-1, both set stock to N-1, and both return true. Previously reserve was synchronous, so that interleaving was impossible. Result: N successful reservations decrement stock by 1 (lost update / oversell).

findings.title: Update retry sleep to match millisecond backoff units
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() previously returned seconds capped at 30 (attempt 0 → 1, attempt ≥5 → 30). Callers converted to ms with * 1000. This change returns ms capped at 30_000 (attempt 0 → 1000, attempt ≥5 → 30000) and schedulePoll was updated, but retry still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000) where sleep() is setTimeout ms. Attempt 0 now waits 1_000_000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s; a capped attempt waits 30_000_000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Retries become effectively stuck.

findings.title: Drop the extra * 1000 in retry now that backoff returns ms
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() used to return seconds (cap 30); both callers converted with * 1000. This PR returns milliseconds (cap 30_000) and updates schedulePoll, but retry still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). sleep() already treats its argument as ms, so attempt 0 waits 1_000_000ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1s, and the cap waits 30_000_000ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30s. Retry is effectively stalled.

findings.title: Stop scaling retry sleep after backoff switched to ms
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() used to return seconds capped at 30 (e.g. attempt 0 → 1, attempt ≥5 → 30). This PR returns milliseconds capped at 30_000 and updates schedulePoll to pass that value straight to setTimeout. retry.ts is unchanged and still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000), where sleep already takes milliseconds. After the unit change, attempt 0 waits 1_000_000ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1s, and the cap waits 30_000_000ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30s. Poll delays stay correct; retry delays are 1000× too long on every failed attempt.

findings.title: Propagate file Close errors from Save after Flush
findings.whyItBreaks: On the success path, Save previously returned f.Close() after Flush. Close can surface delayed write failures (ENOSPC, NFS, etc.). defer f.Close() drops that error, and the function now returns only w.Flush(), so a failed persist is indistinguishable from success for any caller of the exported Save API.

findings.title: Propagate Close error after Flush instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: Save previously ended with return f.Close() after a successful bufio flush, so a Close failure (EIO, NFS, delayed write) was returned to the caller. The new path always defer f.Close() (error ignored) and return w.Flush(); if Flush succeeds, Save returns nil even when Close fails. Save is exported, so every caller is forced to conflate that failure with a successful write.

findings.title: Propagate file Close error after Flush instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: On the success path, Save previously returned f.Close() (base store/save.go:24), so a close-time I/O error (ENOSPC, NFS, already-closed, delayed writeback) reached the caller. The new body always defer f.Close() (error ignored) and return w.Flush(). After a successful Flush that Close error is dropped and Save returns nil, so an exported caller must treat a failed persist as success. Write/Flush failure paths already ignored Close; only the happy path changed.

findings.title: Stop dropping the last row of every page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval (end = min(start+page_size, row_count)), matching the old page_window loop range(start, end). The new loop uses range(start, end-1), so the last index of every non-empty page is omitted. Concrete: rows=['A','B','C'], page_index=0, page_size=3 → start=0,end=3 → range(0,2) returns ['A','B'] (missing 'C'). A 1-row last page (start=end-1) becomes range(start,start)=[] so that row disappears entirely. render_page/summarize therefore emit incomplete pages and skip the last 1-based number on each page.

findings.title: Do not drop the last row of each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds documents and returns a half-open [start, end) interval (start = page_index * page_size, end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), matching the previous range(start, end) loop. page_window now iterates range(start, end - 1), so index end-1 is omitted. Substitution: rows=['a','b','c'], page_size=2 → page 0 yields ['a'] not ['a','b']; page 1 yields [] not ['c']. With page_size=1, end = start+1 so every page is empty. render_page and summarize consume that window, so numbered output and multi-page summaries silently lose the last item of each page.

findings.title: Include the last row in page_window's range
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds documents and returns a half-open [start, end) interval (start = page_index * page_size, end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), matching the pre-change loop range(start, end). page_window now loops range(start, end - 1), so index end-1 is never collected. Concrete substitution: rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2 → page 0 yields ['a'] not ['a','b']; page 1 yields ['c'] not ['c','d']; page 2 (the 1-row remainder) yields [] not ['e']. render_page and summarize both consume that window, so displayed pages omit those rows and numbering skips them.

findings.title: Restore TTL freshness check in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: get() now returns a value only when Date.now() - storedAt > ttlMs, otherwise it deletes the entry and returns null. A just-set key has age ≈ 0, so 0 > ttlMs is false: set() then get() always misses and removes the live entry. Once age exceeds ttlMs, get() returns the expired value instead of evicting. Fresh hits become misses; stale data is served.

findings.title: Do not splice jobs while forEach-ing pruneDone
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#forEach captures length up front and always increments the index. splice(index, 1) shifts the next job into the current index, so that job is never visited. Adjacent done jobs therefore survive: pruneDone([{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]) keeps the second done job. The rewrite also mutates the caller-owned array (filter previously returned a new list).

findings.title: Restore TTL freshness check in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness predicate was flipped from age < ttlMs to age > ttlMs. A just-written entry (age ≈ 0) takes the else branch, is deleted, and returns null. An entry past ttlMs takes the true branch and is returned. get() therefore misses on live keys and serves stale values.

findings.title: Do not splice the job array while forEach iterates
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach walks increasing indices while splice(index,1) shifts later elements left, so the job that moves into the removed index is never visited. Consecutive done jobs are only partially removed (e.g. [{done:true},{done:true}] returns one leftover done job). Unlike the previous filter, this also mutates the caller's array.

findings.title: Restore TtlCache.get to treat age < ttl as a hit
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness predicate was flipped from `age < ttlMs` (return value) to `age > ttlMs` (return value). For any positive TTL, a just-`set` entry has age ≈ 0, so `0 > ttlMs` is false: `get` deletes the entry and returns null. Expired entries (`age > ttlMs`) are returned instead of being evicted. The class's only read path cannot serve a live value.

findings.title: Do not splice jobs inside pruneDone's forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: `filter` built a new array of `!job.done`. The replacement `forEach` + `splice(index, 1)` mutates the caller's array and skips the next element after each removal (forEach still advances). Example: `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]` becomes `[{done:true},{done:false}]` — a done job remains. Adjacent done jobs are never fully pruned.

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard in averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `if (rows.length === 0) return 0` lets `rows.reduce(..., 0) / rows.length` run on `[]`, which is `0 / 0` → `NaN` in JavaScript. The exported function previously returned a finite `0` for no rows; callers that display, compare, serialize, or accumulate the result now get a poison value (`NaN !== 0`, JSON/`Number` operations fail).

findings.title: Stop busiest from sorting the caller’s array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort` mutates its receiver. The previous `[...rows].sort(...)` copied first; `rows.sort(...)` now reorders the caller-owned array as a side effect while returning the max row. Any later use of that same array (original insertion order, secondary stats, UI lists) sees a different order even though the documented result is only `Row | null`.

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard so averageAmount does not return NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array early return was removed. On rows=[], reduce(..., 0) yields 0, then total / rows.length is 0/0, which is NaN in JavaScript. The previous public contract returned 0; NaN will poison any later arithmetic, display, or persistence of the average.

findings.title: Copy before sort in busiest so caller arrays are not mutated
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver. The old body ranked a shallow copy ([...rows].sort(...)); the new body sorts `rows` in place, so the caller’s array order changes after busiest(rows), and frozen arrays throw. The returned max row is otherwise the same, so the side effect is easy to miss.

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard in averageAmount to avoid NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-length early return was removed. For rows=[], reduce(..., 0) yields 0 and `0 / rows.length` is `0 / 0` → NaN. Callers that previously received 0 now get a poisonous NaN (every equality fails; later arithmetic/JSON stay corrupted).

findings.title: Copy before sort in busiest; do not mutate caller rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates in place. Dropping `[...rows]` means busiest reorders the caller-owned array by descending amount. Any later iteration, display, or persistence of that same array uses the shuffled order; a frozen/readonly array now throws.

findings.title: Restore numeric sort in rankScores; default sort is lexicographic
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator stringifies elements. Replacing `sort((a, b) => b - a)` with `sort(); reverse();` ranks by UTF-16 order, not numeric descending. Concrete case: scores [10, 2, 30], n=2. String sort+reverse yields [30, 2, 10], cutoff=2; filter `score >= 2` then `slice(0, 2)` keeps the first two original players (10 and 2) and drops 30. Numeric descending would yield [30, 10, 2], cutoff=10, keeping 10 and 30. Same failure for mixed digit lengths and negatives (e.g. [-1, -10, 5] string-reverse is [5, -10, -1], cutoff=-10, so the highest score can be sliced off). formatBoard renders that wrong set.

findings.title: Restore numeric sort in rankScores; default sort is lexicographic
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no compareFn stringifies elements and orders by UTF-16. The old `(a, b) => b - a` ranked by numeric score; `sort(); reverse();` ranks by string instead. That cutoff is then used as the nth-highest score. Example: players [{name:'a',score:2},{name:'b',score:10}] with n=1 → scores [2,10] become [10,2] ("10" < "2"), reverse yields [2,10], cutoff=2, filter keeps both, slice(0,1) returns score 2 instead of 10. Same failure for any scores with different digit lengths or signs (e.g. 100 vs 20 vs 3; -1 vs -10).

findings.title: Restore numeric sort in rankScores
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparefn orders by ToString lexicographic order, not numeric order. rankScores then reverse()s that string order and topPlayers takes cutoff at index min(n, length)-1. For players [{name:'a',score:20},{name:'b',score:100},{name:'c',score:3}] and n=1, scores sort to [100,20,3] then reverse to [3,20,100], cutoff is 3, filter keeps everyone, and slice(0,1) returns score 20 instead of 100. The previous comparator (b-a) ranked numerically descending; any mixed digit-length scores (10 vs 9, 100 vs 20, etc.) now mis-rank.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook HMAC verify
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the sole authenticity check for handle() (401 vs processor(payload)). hmac.compare_digest is the constant-time primitive for HMAC hex digests; `str == str` is not (CPython can length-check then short-circuit / libc memcmp). An attacker who can time handle/verify can recover expected hexdigest and forge payloads that pass the 401 gate. `==` also delegates to given_signature.__eq__ when types differ, so a non-str object with an always-true __eq__ authenticates; compare_digest raised TypeError instead.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the only auth check before handle() runs processor(payload). hmac.compare_digest was replaced with str ==, which short-circuits on the first differing character. signature_of() always returns a 64-char SHA-256 hex digest, so an attacker who can measure handle()/verify() latency can recover the expected digest character-by-character, then present that digest as given_signature and pass the gate. Valid honest signatures still compare equal, so functional tests will not catch this.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC compare in webhook verify
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the webhook auth gate (handle() 401 vs processor). Replacing hmac.compare_digest with str == lets Python short-circuit on the first mismatched hex character of the SHA-256 digest, so an attacker who can measure handle()/verify() latency can recover given_signature byte-by-byte and forge a payload that is accepted.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the ledger INSERT and both account UPDATEs ran in one db.transaction() block, so they committed or rolled back together. The refactor leaves only _record_ledger inside the with block; _apply_balances runs after the context exits, so the ledger row is already committed. A crash, exception, or connection drop in either UPDATE then leaves a durable ledger entry with no (or only a debit) balance change. The two UPDATEs are also no longer atomic with each other, so a failure between debit and credit permanently destroys funds.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor extracts helpers but leaves `_apply_balances` outside `with db.transaction()`. The ledger INSERT therefore commits when the `with` block exits, then the two account UPDATEs run in autocommit. If either UPDATE fails or the process dies after the commit, a ledger row exists without matching balances. The two UPDATEs are also not atomic with each other: a crash after the debit and before the credit destroys funds. Previously all three statements ran in the same transaction.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Base `transfer()` applied the ledger INSERT and both account UPDATEs in one `with db.transaction()` so they committed or rolled back together. Head still commits `_record_ledger` on leaving that block, then calls `_apply_balances` afterward. If either UPDATE fails, the connection drops, or the process crashes after the `with` exits, the ledger already has a posted transfer while balances are unchanged; if the debit UPDATE succeeds and the credit UPDATE then fails, funds are removed from `from_acct` and never added to `to_acct`. Concurrent readers can also observe a committed ledger row before balances move.

findings.title: Keep billingDay on UTC, not process-local calendar
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given Date always mapped to one YYYY-MM-DD. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which are the host timezone. Example: 2024-01-01T00:30:00.000Z is billing day 2024-01-01 in UTC but 2023-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles. sameBillingDay compares those strings, so two instants that share a UTC day (or that straddle a local midnight) are classified differently than before. Process-local time is also not a customer timezone, so this is not a valid 'bill in local time' implementation — results change across developer machines, CI, and regions.

findings.title: Restore UTC calendar components in billingDay
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay previously keyed the UTC calendar date (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate). It now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which are host-local. For 2026-01-01T00:30:00.000Z, UTC is 2026-01-01, but America/New_York is 2025-12-31. sameBillingDay(a,b) at line 8 then classifies two instants on the same UTC day that straddle local midnight as different days (and the reverse near local midnight). Stored UTC billing-day keys will miss after deploy on any non-UTC host.

findings.title: Restore UTC getters in billingDay
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay previously keyed YYYY-MM-DD from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the same instant maps to a different calendar day whenever the process TZ is not UTC. sameBillingDay compares those strings, so two timestamps on the same UTC day that straddle local midnight now compare false (previously true), and two timestamps on different UTC days that share a local date now compare true. That mis-buckets any billing window, invoice period, or usage key derived from this export.

findings.title: Include tenant in memo key to avoid cross-tenant cache hits
findings.whyItBreaks: memo is a process-wide Map. Keying only by account means readProfile('acme','alice', fetch) stores that Profile under 'alice'; a later readProfile('globex','alice', fetch) hits the cache and returns acme's Profile (tenant, displayName, and all) without calling fetchProfile. The original `${tenant}:${account}` key was the isolation boundary; fetchProfile still receives tenant, so only the cache path is wrong.

findings.title: Restore tenant in the profile memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile(tenant, account, fetchProfile) still takes tenant as part of the lookup identity and still fetches with it on miss, but the module-level memo now keys only on account. After a cache fill for (tenantA, accountX), a later readProfile(tenantB, accountX, ...) hits memo.get(accountX) and returns tenantA's Profile (including displayName and tenant) without calling fetchProfile. Same-account IDs across tenants collide in the process-wide Map.

findings.title: Restore tenant in memo key to stop cross-tenant cache hits
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level memo is now keyed only by `account`. After tenant A caches account X, a later `readProfile(B, X, …)` takes the `if (cached) return cached` branch and returns A's Profile (A's `tenant` and `displayName`) without calling `fetchProfile`. The previous `${tenant}:${account}` key existed specifically because Profile identity is tenant-scoped.

findings.title: Do not swallow missing-key errors as empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: load previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when Map.get returned undefined. The new catch-all returns "", which is also a legitimate stored Map value, so missing keys, unexpected store.get failures, and real empty values are indistinguishable. loadAll maps load over keys, so it no longer fail-fasts and now emits "" for absent keys as if they were present.

findings.title: Do not swallow load() failures as empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported load() previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when store.get returned undefined. The new catch-all returns "". Map<string,string> can already store "" as a real value, so callers cannot tell missing/error from a present empty string. loadAll maps through load, so a missing key no longer fail-fasts the batch and is persisted in the result array as "". The catch also hides non-missing throws (e.g. store.get on a non-Map).

findings.title: Do not map missing-key errors to empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported load() previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when Map.get returned undefined, and that exception propagated to callers (including exported loadAll). The new catch-all returns "". loadAll maps every key through load, so a missing key no longer fails the batch and the result array contains "". Empty string is also a legitimate stored value (Map.get returns "" after set(key, "")), so callers cannot distinguish failure from real data and will use the fallback as a stored value. The same catch also swallows any unexpected throw from store.get.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows timeout and errors as a void return
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported function returns on deadline, catch-all continues on any throw from fn(), and then returns void after the loop. Success, timeout, and terminal failure are the same observable result (undefined, no throw), so callers are forced to treat failure as completed work.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground failure after timeout or exhausted retries
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a new exported path. fn() success returns void; fn() throw is caught and continued; retry exhaustion falls off the function with void; deadline uses a bare return. Those terminals are identical, so a caller cannot tell completed work from a failed or timed-out retry and will treat failure as success.

findings.title: Rethrow retryBackground failures instead of returning void
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is exported and returns void on every outcome. fn() exceptions are caught and dropped; on deadline (line 23) or after retries exhaust (line 31) it returns without throwing. Callers cannot tell success from failure and will treat unfinished work as done. TypeScript void does not mean 'cannot throw'; a retry helper's terminal failure signal is a thrown error.

findings.title: Coerce Field value to string before reading .length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, but the label interpolates value.length. Numbers have no length property, so a numeric prop (e.g. 123) yields defaultValue "len=undefined" instead of a character count.

findings.title: Coerce numeric Field value before reading .length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, but the body interpolates value.length. Numbers have no length property, so value={42} sets the input defaultValue to "len=undefined" instead of a character/digit length such as "len=2".

findings.title: Coerce Field value before reading .length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, but the label interpolates value.length. Primitive numbers have no length, so any numeric prop (including 0) yields undefined and the input's defaultValue becomes the string "len=undefined" instead of a digit/character count. This is the exported public contract: callers who pass a number, as the new type invites, get a wrong displayed value.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN into GitHub Actions logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step copies ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} into env TOKEN and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN". That writes the live secret to the job log. GitHub redaction is explicitly best-effort (it fails for short values, transformed values, and runner/step debug), and this workflow runs on every push with logs readable by anyone with Actions access. A deploy token in logs is a credential leak; the following make build step does not even receive TOKEN, so the print is not required for deploy.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN into deploy workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects secrets.TOKEN into TOKEN and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN", so the live credential is written to the Actions job log on every push. Workflow logs are readable by anyone with repository read access (and by the public if the repo is public). GitHub log redaction is best-effort and fails for short, structured, or shell-transformed values, so this is a credential leak in a deploy pipeline rather than a debug no-op.

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN into GitHub Actions logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step sets TOKEN from secrets.TOKEN and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN", which expands the live credential onto step stdout. Actions persists stdout as job logs (readable by anyone with log access; on a public repo, by anyone). GitHub's log masking is best-effort and documented as insufficient: short, transformed, or debug-emitted values can appear unredacted, and the secret is also present in the step process environment/argv.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer on git spawnSync
findings.whyItBreaks: Node spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1MiB. runGithub still calls git(['diff', mergeBase, headSha]), and lockfile/generated-code patches routinely exceed 1MiB. On overflow Node kills git (ENOBUFS, status null); git() treats that as failure and runGithub’s catch posts a failed check with exitCode 1 instead of reviewing. gh/ghText still pass 64MiB, so this drop is inconsistent and regresses large PRs that previously succeeded.

findings.title: Assign mergeBase to bundle.baseSha so it matches the patch
findings.whyItBreaks: Shorthand `baseSha` passes PR_BASE_SHA || merge-base(origin/main, HEAD), not `git merge-base $baseSha $headSha`. patch and changedFiles are still computed from mergeBase. When PR_BASE_SHA is GitHub pull_request.base.sha (base-branch tip) and the PR has diverged, merge-base(tip, head) !== tip, so review(bundle) receives a comparison SHA that does not correspond to the included patch (two-dot vs three-dot range).

findings.title: Restore git spawnSync maxBuffer; 1MiB default kills large PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1024*1024. runGithub loads the full PR patch through this helper via git(['diff', mergeBase, headSha], cwd) at line 140. When stdout exceeds 1MiB, Node kills git (ENOBUFS, status null), git() throws on status !== 0, and the catch at 182–193 posts a failed check and sets exitCode 1. The previous 64MiB cap (still used by gh/ghText) allowed those reviews to succeed; lockfile and generated-file PRs routinely exceed 1MiB.

findings.title: Pass mergeBase as bundle.baseSha; shorthand uses the unmerged base
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is PR_BASE_SHA or merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) (line 138). mergeBase is then git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) (line 139) specifically because those can differ. patch and changedFiles still use mergeBase (140–141), but object shorthand now stores the pre-merge-base SHA on the bundle. When PR_BASE_SHA is GitHub's pull_request.base.sha and the PR is behind main, merge-base(baseSha, headSha) !== baseSha, so review(bundle) receives a left-side SHA that does not match patch: two-dot git diff bundle.baseSha bundle.headSha includes unrelated main-branch commits.

findings.title: Restore git spawnSync maxBuffer; 1MiB default fails large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync maxBuffer defaults to 1024*1024. git() is what captures `git diff mergeBase headSha` (the full PR patch). Diffs over 1MiB (lockfiles, generated files, large PRs) terminate the child with ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER; git() throws on status!==0; runGithub posts a failed check and sets exitCode=1. The previous 64MiB cap (still used by gh()/ghText()) let those reviews finish.

findings.title: Keep Codex exec pinned to read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` still `spawnSync`s `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and only returns the last-message text. Headless `exec` does not prompt for approval, so sandbox policy is the only write/exec brake. Removing `-s read-only` leaves sandbox to the CLI default and `~/.codex` / project `config.toml` (`workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`), which can write and run commands in the target repo. `--output-last-message` is written by the parent CLI into a temp dir, so the helper does not need a writable workspace sandbox.

findings.title: Dropping -s read-only lets Codex mutate the reviewed repo
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` still `spawnSync`s `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and the prompt on stdin, but no longer passes `-s read-only`. `codex exec` is non-interactive (no human approval), so sandbox mode is the only write/exec brake. Without the flag, policy falls through to CLI defaults, `~/.codex/config.toml` `sandbox_mode`, and trusted-directory Agent/workspace-write presets. The child can then edit the target repo, run mutating commands, and (depending on config) use the network — the explicit read-only pin was the only control in this wrapper.

findings.title: Pin Codex exec sandbox to read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns headless `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath`. The previous argv included `-s read-only`, which is a CLI flag and therefore outranks `~/.codex/config.toml` / project config / built-in defaults. After this change the sandbox flag is absent, so `sandbox_mode` falls through to config or Codex's local default (commonly `workspace-write`). `codex exec` cannot prompt for approval, so that looser policy lets the model edit the workspace and run local commands with no human gate. That is a real policy regression on an exported runner, not a no-op default.

findings.title: Restore merge-base for GitHub PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub still sets baseSha from PR_BASE_SHA (GitHub pull_request.base.sha is the base-branch tip, not the merge-base) and headSha from PR_HEAD_SHA. The removed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` was what turned that tip into a three-dot PR range. `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot tree diff: once main has moved, the patch includes reverse hunks for base-only commits and can drop files whose net two-dot diff is empty. review(bundle) at line 176 then reviews non-PR changes; changedFileSet (line 57) builds the same wrong path set, so inlineComments (line 63) mis-filters, and postReview still attaches comments to commit_id=headSha (line 85) even though the patch was computed against HEAD.

findings.title: Use merge-base..headSha for the PR patch, not baseSha..HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub used to review git diff $(merge-base baseSha headSha) headSha (three-dot vs the commit later posted as commit_id). It now runs git diff baseSha HEAD and changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha), which is git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD. PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip, not the fork point: when main has moved, two-dot includes reverse diffs of main-only commits and omits PR changes that already match current main. The right side is also HEAD, which in Actions is often the merge commit while headSha stays PR_HEAD_SHA; hunk line numbers then do not exist on commit_id, so inlineComments/postReview attach comments to the wrong commit (or the existing catch posts a body with no inline comments). Up-to-date PRs where baseSha ancestors HEAD and HEAD==headSha are unchanged; the live diverged-PR path is not.

findings.title: Restore merge-base vs headSha for the GitHub PR patch
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub still treats headSha as the PR commit (bundle.headSha, reviews commit_id, check head_sha) and still takes PR_BASE_SHA as a possibly non-ancestor base tip (otherwise the old merge-base(baseSha, headSha) step would have been redundant). Replacing that with git diff baseSha HEAD is a two-dot tree diff against the checkout: when PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip and the PR is behind (typical Actions github.event.pull_request.base.sha), the patch and changedFileSet include reverse diffs of commits that landed on the base after the fork point — files the PR never touched. review() then flags those files; inlineComments lets them through changedPaths.has(f.file); GitHub rejects comments that are not on the PR three-dot diff, and postReview's catch posts a review with no inline comments. Separately, when PR_HEAD_SHA != HEAD (default pull_request checkout is the merge commit), line numbers come from HEAD while commit_id stays headSha, so comments target the wrong commit.

findings.title: Restore function replacers; string replace interpolates $ in patches
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacementValue runs ECMAScript GetSubstitution: `$$` becomes `$`, `$&` becomes the matched placeholder (`{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}`), `$`` becomes the prefix, `$'` becomes the suffix. The base used zero-arg replacer functions so JSON/patch text was inserted literally. `bundle.patch` is a raw git diff; JS/shell/Make changes routinely contain those sequences (e.g. `$&` in a replace call, `$$` in a Makefile). JSON.stringify does not escape `$`, so the same rewrite hits the serialized bundle and candidate findings. The corrupted strings are passed to runCodex, so the model reviews the wrong input and can emit a wrong verdict/findings with no error.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so patch $ sequences stay literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement runs GetSubstitution: $$ → $, $& → the matched placeholder, $` → template prefix, $' → template suffix. The previous `() => value` form inserts the string unchanged. bundle.patch (and JSON.stringify of bundle/candidate, which embed that patch) routinely contain those sequences (bash $$, $'...', perl/JS $&, Makefiles). The critic therefore reviews a mangled patch (e.g. `echo $$` becomes `echo $`; `$&` becomes the literal `{{PATCH}}`; `$'` splices the rest of critic.md into the payload). runCodex then sees the corrupted prompt.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid $-substitution in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacer via GetSubstitution even when the search is a literal. `$$` becomes `$`, `$&` becomes `{{PATCH}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`, `$`` inserts the prompt prefix, and `$'` inserts the suffix. The previous `() => value` form inserted the text verbatim. `bundle.patch` is raw diff text (and JSON.stringify(bundle) embeds that patch); git diffs of shell/JS/Perl/regex routinely contain those sequences, so both Codex prompts are silently mangled before runCodex.

findings.title: Keep commit_id on the fallback review POST
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview's catch path is the live fallback when the JSON review POST fails (typical GitHub 422 on inline comment positions). That path still submits event (including REQUEST_CHANGES) and body, but this diff removes commit_id=${headSha}. GitHub's create-review API then defaults commit_id to the PR's most recent commit, not the SHA in the review bundle. The same headSha is still sent on the JSON path (line 89) and as check-run head_sha (line 128), so a fallback review/REQUEST_CHANGES can be stored against a different commit than the one that was actually analyzed—including a commit pushed after analysis started.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating P1 defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw on non-objects and on invalid/missing severity, category, file, title, whyItBreaks, suggestedFix, and non-positive/non-finite line numbers. It now substitutes sentinels: invalid severity → "P1" (schema.ts:98), invalid/untrimmed category → "bug" (schema.ts:100-102), missing title → "Untitled finding" (schema.ts:99), missing file → "" (schema.ts:103), missing/invalid lineStart/lineEnd → 0 or NaN (schema.ts:104-105), empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix (schema.ts:107-108). normalizeReview always maps findings through this (schema.ts:131) and the strict=false drop-invalid path was removed, so a malformed element is emitted as a real P1 bug. Callers of this exported API cannot tell failure from a legitimate finding; JSON.stringify will also turn NaN line numbers into null.

findings.title: Stop mapping malformed findings to lookalike P1 defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to throw on non-object input, invalid severity/category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-positive lineStart/lineEnd. The new body maps those failures to real-looking values: severity "P1" (line 98), title "Untitled finding" or "" (line 99), category "bug" (lines 100-102), file "" (line 103), lineStart/lineEnd 0 or NaN (lines 104-105), empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix (lines 107-108). Callers can no longer tell a parse failure from a legitimate finding. normalizeReview (line 131) always maps through this coercer and dropped the strict=false path that omitted bad items, so garbage is now persisted as P1/bug findings. Separately, the object guard was removed: raw null/undefined throws TypeError on raw.severity (line 96) instead of Error("malformed finding: not an object"), and a null entry in raw.findings now crashes the whole review parse.

findings.title: Do not fabricate P1 findings from malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to throw on non-objects, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-positive/non-finite line numbers. The new body maps those failures to a complete Finding: invalid/missing severity → "P1", invalid category → "bug", missing title → "Untitled finding", missing file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix → "", missing lines → 0, and Number("x")/Infinity pass through as NaN/Infinity because isFinite was removed. normalizeReview always does raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) and dropped both the default strict throw path and the strict=false drop path, so a raw {} or {severity:"high"} is stored as a real P1 bug. Exported callers cannot distinguish LLM garbage from a legitimate P1.

findings.title: Restore repo target for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the live workflow_dispatch path: EVENT_HEAD is empty because github.event.pull_request is absent, so refs are resolved only via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"`. That step runs before actions/checkout, so there is no local git remote. `gh` does not read GITHUB_REPOSITORY (only GH_REPO or `-R`); issue cli/cli#3556 is still open and `gh help environment` documents GH_REPO alone. Without `-R`/`GH_REPO`, `gh pr view` errors (empty workspace) or uses leftover remotes on this self-hosted runner. The invocations are inside `echo "head=$(gh ...)"` / `echo "base=$(gh ...)"`; under Actions' `bash -e`, a failing command substitution used as an echo argument does not fail the step, so GITHUB_OUTPUT can record empty head/base. Checkout then treats an empty `ref` as the dispatch SHA (typically default branch), and Needlefish still runs `--pr $PR_NUM` against those wrong SHAs.

findings.title: Keep -R on pre-checkout gh pr view
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the workflow_dispatch path (EVENT_HEAD is empty because github.event.pull_request is unset). It runs before actions/checkout, so $GITHUB_WORKSPACE has no git remotes. gh pr view without -R/--repo only accepts GH_REPO or local remotes (OverrideBaseRepoFunc); it does not read GITHUB_REPOSITORY. Result: gh fails with 'not a git repository' (or, on a dirty self-hosted workspace, may bind to leftover remotes). head/base outputs are never produced, so Checkout PR head never gets the intended SHAs.

findings.title: Restore gh -R; workflow_dispatch cannot resolve PR SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the workflow_dispatch path: github.event.pull_request is absent, so EVENT_HEAD is empty and [ -n "$EVENT_HEAD" ] is false. This step runs before actions/checkout, so cwd has no git remotes. gh resolves the repo only from -R/--repo or GH_REPO (cli OverrideBaseRepoFunc); it does not read Actions' GITHUB_REPOSITORY. After dropping REPO and -R "$REPO", `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` cannot determine the repository, so head/base outputs are not produced and Checkout PR head cannot fetch the intended SHAs. The pull_request path is unaffected because it uses EVENT_HEAD/EVENT_BASE.

findings.title: Do not map malformed review output to an empty successful review
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously threw on non-object input and on missing/non-string summary or missing/non-array findings, checked, or residual_risks. Those throws are gone: null, a string, {}, or a payload whose findings is not an array all become { summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] }. That shape is a legitimate “clean” review, so callers can no longer tell a failed/unusable model payload from a real empty review and will treat the fallback as success (no findings). The function is exported; the unusable contract is the defect even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Restore malformed-review throws; empty defaults hide failures
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously threw on non-object input and on missing/non-string summary or missing/non-array findings, checked, or residual_risks, so callers could treat malformed model output as a failed review. The new body substitutes Array.isArray(raw?.findings) ? map : [], the same for residual_risks and checked, and String(raw?.summary ?? ""). Substitutions: normalizeReview(null)/undefined/"x" and normalizeReview({}) all return {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}, which is also the shape of a valid empty/pass review. Failure and success are no longer distinguishable; an exported parser that used to surface Error("malformed review output: ...") now reports a clean no-finding result.

findings.title: Do not coerce malformed reviews into an empty success
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview previously threw on non-object input, non-string summary, or missing/non-array findings, checked, or residual_risks. Those Errors were the only failure signal. The new code maps every one of those cases to { summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] }, which is also a legitimate no-finding review. The function is exported, so every caller is forced to treat parse failure as a successful empty review (false-green).

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still runs on workflow_dispatch (on.workflow_dispatch + job if + required pr_number input), but the deleted 'Resolve PR refs' else-branch was the only path that called `gh pr view` when github.event.pull_request is absent. On dispatch, github.event.pull_request.* is empty: checkout `ref` becomes github.ref (the branch selected at dispatch, typically the default branch, not the PR head); BASE_REF becomes the hardcoded 'main'; PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA become empty strings. The review then installs and executes src/cli.ts from the wrong tree (this repo's self-review mode depends on checking out the PR head) and cannot pin the PR range. pull_request events still have those fields and are unaffected.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still runs on workflow_dispatch (on.workflow_dispatch with required pr_number at L10-14, job if at L24, --pr still takes github.event.inputs.pr_number at L47). A workflow_dispatch payload has no github.event.pull_request, so the new coalesces are empty: checkout ref becomes github.ref (the 'use workflow from' branch, typically the default branch) instead of the PR head SHA the removed `gh pr view` else-branch resolved; BASE_REF becomes hardcoded 'main' rather than the PR's base.ref; PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA become empty. This workflow's own comment states the PR checkout's src/ is the tool, so Install + cli.ts execute the wrong tree while still claiming to review that PR.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch no longer resolves PR head/base SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still triggers on workflow_dispatch (required pr_number) and the job if still allows that event, but the only dispatch path that resolved the PR (gh pr view when EVENT_HEAD was empty) was removed. On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is unset, so checkout uses github.ref (the selected workflow branch, typically default) instead of the PR head, git fetch falls back to origin/main instead of the PR base, and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty strings. The CLI is still invoked with --pr ${{ github.event.inputs.pr_number }}, so the job silently reviews the wrong commits (or empty SHAs) rather than failing closed. Same-repo pull_request webhooks still populate those fields; fork PRs skipped by the job if, and any manual re-review, are now broken.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer on git spawnSync
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1024*1024. git() captures a full `git diff BASE HEAD` as a string in runLocal; any unified diff over 1MiB now kills the child (ENOBUFS / status null) and git() throws, so local review never starts. The previous 64MiB cap (still set on gh() at L33-36) allowed those reviews. Lockfile and generated-file PRs routinely exceed 1MiB.

findings.title: Restore git spawnSync 64MiB maxBuffer for large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync now omits maxBuffer, so Node applies MAX_BUFFER = 1024 * 1024 (1MiB). runLocal captures the full PR with git(['diff', baseSha, 'HEAD']). Any unified diff over 1MiB hits spawnSync's stdoutLen > maxBuffer path (child killed, error ENOBUFS / status null). git() then throws on status !== 0 and runLocal never builds the bundle. Typical lockfile/refactor PRs exceed 1MiB; the previous 64MiB cap (still present on gh()) handled them.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer or diffs over 1MiB fail
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1MiB. git() is the local adapter's path for `git diff base HEAD` (runLocal line 100). When stdout exceeds 1MiB, Node kills the child (status=null, error ENOBUFS); `res.status !== 0` then throws and review never runs. That previously succeeded up to 64MiB. Sibling gh() still sets maxBuffer 64MiB, so this is not an intentional global cap.

findings.title: Stop posting review crashes as a passing GitHub check
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path still titles the check 'Needlefish: review failed' and says the PR did NOT pass, and still sets process.exitCode=1, but postCheck now sends conclusion "neutral". GitHub documents successful required-check statuses as success, skipped, and neutral. The named check this adapter publishes (name: "Needlefish") will therefore satisfy branch protection / required checks when review() throws, which is indistinguishable from the pre-existing needs_human→neutral path and weaker than the previous failure conclusion. The workflow job failing is a different check name; anything that requires "Needlefish" will not see a failure.

findings.title: Keep error-path check conclusion as failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path still titles the check 'Needlefish: review failed' and says the review 'did NOT pass this PR', but conclusion is now 'neutral'. GitHub documents required-check success as success, skipped, and neutral, so a required check named Needlefish will allow merge when review() (or postReview/postCheck) throws. That is also the same conclusion as needs_human, so a crash is indistinguishable from a completed non-blocking review on the check run. process.exitCode=1 still fails the Actions job, but the check this adapter posts is the stable Needlefish gate and no longer fails.

findings.title: Keep error-path check conclusion as failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: On review() throw, postCheck now sends conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". GitHub required-status-check success set is success|skipped|neutral, so a required check named Needlefish no longer blocks merge when the reviewer crashes. That is the same conclusion already used for needs_human (VERDICT_CONCLUSION), so branch protection cannot tell a crash from an advisory result. The check title/summary still say the review failed and did not pass, and process.exitCode=1 only fails a separately named Actions job—not this check-run.

findings.title: Do not install and run the PR head as the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The job runs on a persistent self-hosted runner and passes GH_TOKEN with pull-requests: write and checks: write into the review step. Before this change, pnpm install and src/cli.ts came from a second checkout of frankekn/needlefish@main (path needlefish/), and the PR SHA was only a data worktree (path target/). Now the PR SHA is the workspace root, so a same-repo branch can (1) execute arbitrary package lifecycle scripts from its lockfile during Install, and (2) replace src/cli.ts so the step that posts reviews/checks attests to the same PR. The job if still skips forks, but anyone who can push a branch in this repo now controls the control that was explicitly designed not to trust PR tool code.

findings.title: Run untrusted PR code as reviewer on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still runs on a persistent self-hosted runner with pull-requests:write and checks:write, and still accepts same-repo pull_request events. This diff drops the second checkout of frankekn/needlefish@main, checks the PR head into $GITHUB_WORKSPACE, runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (lifecycle scripts from the PR lockfile), then executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from that same tree with GH_TOKEN. findings.title: Stop executing PR-head as the reviewer on the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Base checked the PR head out to `target/` as data and installed/ran only `frankekn/needlefish@main` under `needlefish/`, so a PR could not change the reviewer. Head checks out `${{ steps.refs.outputs.head }}` into GITHUB_WORKSPACE, runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` on that tree, then executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` with `GH_TOKEN` (`pull-requests: write`, `checks: write`) on `runs-on: self-hosted`. After merge, any same-repo PR (or `workflow_dispatch`) can run lockfile lifecycle scripts on the persistent runner and replace the reviewer with code that always posts a clean review / green check. The job `if` only skips fork `pull_request` events and does not mitigate this.

findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization; stop defaulting unknown to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding no longer does String(trim).toUpperCase() before the SEVERITIES check, and the fallback changed from P1 to P3. normalizeReview maps untyped JSON through this helper, so values that previously became real severities now fail includes() and are stored as P3: 'p0' was P0 and is now P3; 'P0 ' was P0 and is now P3; missing/invalid was P1 and is now P3. Callers cannot tell a parsed P3 from a failed parse, so a critical finding with ordinary LLM/JSON slop is classified as low-risk.

findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization; stop defaulting unknowns to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview passes untyped JSON findings through normalizeFinding. The old path did String(raw.severity??'').trim().toUpperCase() then allowlisted against SEVERITIES, so 'p0', 'P1 ', and 'p1' became P0/P1, and missing/garbage became P1. The new SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) is case- and whitespace-sensitive, so those inputs miss the allowlist and are stored as the new fallback P3 — a legitimate severity. Callers cannot tell a real P3 from a parse failure, so high-severity issues are persisted and later treated as low-risk.

findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization; stop defaulting mismatches to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview feeds untyped `any` findings into normalizeFinding. Previously severity was `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` then whitelisted, so `p0`, `P0`, and ` P0 ` all became `P0`, and anything else became `P1`. The new `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` check is case- and whitespace-sensitive, and the fallback is `P3`. Substituting live inputs: `raw.severity="p0"` → includes is false → stored severity `P3` (was `P0`); `" P1 "` → `P3` (was `P1`); `undefined`/`""` → `P3` (was `P1`). That silently reclassifies high-severity or missing tokens as the lowest severity on the public parser.

findings.title: Do not pass GitHub tokens into the Codex child env
findings.whyItBreaks: Base cloned process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync, so the Codex child could not see GitHub credentials. Head omits `env`, and Node child_process then inherits the full parent environment. Those tokens are now present in a `codex exec -s read-only` process that takes an arbitrary prompt and returns model output, so a prompt-injection can read or emit the token.

Codex still returns last-message/stdout to the caller, so a prompt-injected dump (or any child use of `gh`/GitHub APIs) can exfiltrate CI tokens that this path was written to withhold.

findings.title: Restore same-repo job if on self-hosted PR execution
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only fork guard on this job. After the deletion the `review` job always runs on `pull_request`. It checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, runs `pnpm install` (lifecycle scripts), then executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from that checkout on `runs-on: self-hosted`. A fork PR can therefore run arbitrary code on a persistent runner (host credentials, network, later privileged jobs). That is the documented self-hosted + untrusted-PR anti-pattern; the file comment even describes this workflow as executing the PR's own `src/` as the tool.

findings.title: Accept 0ms env durations instead of substituting fallbacks
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`. `Number("0")` is finite and was previously returned as 0; it now fails the check and returns `fallbackMs`. Live consumers are `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS` (fallback 5000) used as the SIGTERM→SIGKILL `setTimeout` delay and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS` (fallback 2000) used as the SIGKILL→`finish` delay. An operator setting either env to `0` (or ` 0 `) used to schedule those steps on the next turn; they now wait 5000ms / 2000ms. That inverts the usual meaning of an explicit 0 delay (skip/minimize the wait) into the full default wait, with no error. `setTimeout(..., 0)` is a valid delay; the exported helper still returns 0 when the fallback itself is 0, so 0 is not treated as an unusable timer value elsewhere.

findings.title: Honor 0 ms as a valid runner duration
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`. `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` used to return 0 and feed `setTimeout(..., 0)` (immediate SIGKILL after SIGTERM, and immediate give-up after SIGKILL). They now fail the guard and become 5000 and 2000, so operators cannot disable those waits and every timeout pays the default delays instead.

findings.title: Treat duration 0 as valid, not as fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`. `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` previously meant immediate SIGKILL after SIGTERM and immediate give-up after SIGKILL (`setTimeout(fn, 0)`). They now fail the guard and become 5000ms / 2000ms with no error. Empty/unset already maps to those fallbacks; 0 was the only way to request no wait. The exported parser has the same silent domain change for any caller passing "0".

findings.title: Do not skip changed files outside the top 6 hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge still takes only sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6) and then deep-reviews only that array. The coverage backstop that pushed leftover bundle.changedFiles into a tail hotspot is gone, and nothing records the omission. Any changed path not listed on those 6 hotspots is never sent to deep.md; checked[] only mentions reviewed hotspots; residual_risks is forced to []. isLarge is patch>30000 chars or changedFiles.length>10, so this is the normal large-PR path — the result looks complete while entire files are unreviewed.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual_risks into the critic, not []
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass still returns a RawReview, but only res.findings and res.summary are kept. res.residual_risks is discarded, and candidateMerged hardcodes residual_risks: []. That JSON is the critic's {{FINDINGS}} payload; deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) and ReviewResult.residualRisks then see only whatever the critic emits. Blocking deep residuals (blocks:true) that previously reached the critic can no longer affect the verdict or the public residualRisks list — failure/uncertainty is stored as an empty list. reviewSmall still forwards candidate.residual_risks via JSON.stringify(candidate), so this is a large-path contract break, not a product-wide choice.

findings.title: Deep-review changed files that fall outside the top 6 hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge still caps map hotspots at MAX_HOTSPOTS=6, but the tail-coverage hotspot is gone. Any changed path not listed in those 6 hotspots is never substituted into a deep.md prompt, so it produces no findings and is never critic-reviewed. That was a live path: the map pass is an LLM survey (lossy file assignment) and slice(0,6) drops lower-risk hotspots. Previously uncovered paths were pushed as tail-coverage and deep-reviewed.

findings.title: Pass deep-review residual_risks through to critic and verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass still returns RawReview.residual_risks, but the loop only concatenates findings and candidateMerged hardcodes residual_risks: []. The critic therefore receives an explicit empty list, and deriveVerdict plus ReviewResult.residualRisks only see critic output seeded from that. A deep pass with findings=[] and residual_risks=[{blocks:true}] used to be visible to critic/verdict; now it is indistinguishable from a clean deep pass and a large review can PASS while those blocking gaps are dropped.

findings.title: Keep unmapped changed files in a tail hotspot after the slice
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge is used when changedFiles.length > 10 or the patch is huge (isLarge). Hotspots are then sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) with MAX_HOTSPOTS=6, and only that array is deep-reviewed. The coverage backstop that pushed leftover bundle.changedFiles into a tail hotspot is gone, so files only in dropped hotspot 7+ (or never assigned by map) never appear in any deep prompt. Those files contribute no findings and no coverage note.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual_risks instead of sending the critic []
findings.whyItBreaks: Deep reviews previously appended res.residual_risks (including blocks:true 'could not verify' / failed-pass notes) into candidateMerged, which is JSON.stringified into the critic prompt; deriveVerdict and the returned ReviewResult.residualRisks then see only the critic's residuals. candidateMerged.residual_risks is now hardcoded []. Blocking residuals from successful deep passes never reach the critic, so they cannot appear in pruned.residual_risks. Combined with the missing tail hotspot, an incomplete large review has no in-band blocks:true signal and can PASS.

findings.title: Restore focus/deep on large-PR map bundle and deep {{FOCUS}}
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge runs when patch length > 30000 or changedFiles.length > 10 (isLarge), which is exactly when a caller would set Bundle.focus to steer the MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 map. mapBundle is JSON.stringified into map.md without focus/deep, so the mapper never receives those fields. The per-hotspot deep prompt also no longer replaces {{FOCUS}}, so deep.md is sent with a leftover {{FOCUS}} token instead of bundle.focus ?? "(none)". reviewSmall still JSON.stringifies the full bundle, so the same caller-supplied focus/deep only work on small PRs.

findings.title: Thread focus/deep through large-review map and deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge used to put focus/deep on the map JSON and replace {{FOCUS}} in deep.md with bundle.focus ?? "(none)". This PR deletes those three lines and does not change the prompt templates. The remaining deep.md chain still replaces {{AGENTS}}/{{HOTSPOT}}/{{BASE}}/{{HEAD}}, so {{FOCUS}} now reaches Codex as a literal token instead of the caller’s focus (or "(none)"). mapBundle at lines 83–89 also omits focus/deep, so hotspot selection cannot honor them either. review() still routes large patches to reviewLarge (isLarge at lines 30–32); reviewSmall still JSON.stringifies the full bundle, so the same Bundle.focus/deep inputs remain live on the small path and silently no-op on the large path.

findings.title: Restore focus wiring on large-PR map and deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge used to put bundle.focus (and bundle.deep) on the map payload and substitute {{FOCUS}} with bundle.focus ?? "(none)" in every deep.md prompt. Both wires are gone; prompts/deep.md is not in this diff, so the {{FOCUS}} slot is still in the template. runCodex therefore sees a raw placeholder instead of the caller focus, and the mapper JSON no longer contains focus/deep. reviewSmall still JSON.stringifies the full bundle, so the same Bundle.focus input is honored only on the small path — large PRs silently ignore it. Files are still deep-reviewed (tail-coverage backstop), but hotspot ranking and per-hotspot instructions no longer receive the caller-supplied focus.

findings.title: Carry seconds=60 into minutes in formatDuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from ms, then the remainder is rounded to seconds. For any ms in [n*60000-500, n*60000), Math.round((ms%60000)/1000) is 60 (JS Math.round half-up). 59500 therefore becomes '60s' (minutes=0) and 119500 becomes '1m 60s' (minutes=1). Callers at renderMarkdown stats/total lines emit that string. The previous implementation rounded total seconds first, which correctly produced '1m 0s' and '2m 0s'.

findings.title: Carry remainder seconds when rounding hits 60
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from raw ms, then leftover ms are rounded independently: Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000) is 60 for any leftover in [59500, 60000). That value is interpolated as-is, so 59500ms renders as "60s" and 119500ms as "1m 60s". The previous body rounded total seconds first then split with % 60, so the seconds field was always 0–59 and those inputs rendered as "1m 0s" / "2m 0s".

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds of 60 into the next minute
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are taken with Math.floor(ms / 60000) and seconds are independently Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000). When the remainder is ≥ 59500ms, seconds becomes 60 and minutes is not incremented. Substituting seconds=60 into `minutes > 0` at line 92: 59500ms → minutes=0 → '60s'; 119500ms → minutes=1 → '1m 60s'. The previous implementation rounded total seconds first (Math.round(ms/1000) then floor-divide by 60), which carried those inputs to '1m 0s' and '2m 0s'. Call sites at lines 75 and 80 print this string in review markdown stats, so near-minute LLM/call durations display an invalid time.

findings.title: Reject 0 in parsePositiveInteger to match the contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parser is still named parsePositiveInteger and still throws `${label} requires a positive integer`, but the guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`. Substitution: Number("0") is 0, Number.isInteger(0) is true, and 0 < 0 is false, so the function now returns 0. The same path accepts every string Number() coerces to 0, including "", whitespace, "-0", "0.0", and "0x0" — all of which previously threw. Callers of this public API can no longer treat a successful return as a strictly positive integer.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger to match its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger is exported and still promises a positive integer (symbol name plus the throw text `${label} requires a positive integer`). The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so Number.isInteger(0) passes and the function returns 0. Inputs "0", "+0", "0.0", and "" (Number("") === 0) now succeed instead of throwing. A successful return is no longer guaranteed > 0, so any caller using the result as a count, timeout, or limit will treat zero as valid.

findings.title: Reject 0 in parsePositiveInteger to match its contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parser is named parsePositiveInteger and still throws `${label} requires a positive integer`, but the guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`. Number.isInteger(0) is true and `0 < 0` is false, so input "0" now returns 0 instead of throwing. Number("") and Number(" ") are also 0, so empty/whitespace strings now succeed too. Callers that treat a successful parse as n >= 1 receive 0.
